extracted.intended_audience: novelists and advanced fiction writers interested in point-of-view and dramatization techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on rendering a character's inner life and moral/emotional change by choosing and managing point of view, dramatizing thought as surface imagery, and using scene construction rather than retrospective exposition. Focuses on novel-scale treatment (e.g., The Ambassadors, The Wings of the Dove).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view must match the inner change
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is a story which must obviously be told from Strether's point of view... The change in his purpose is due to a change in his vision, and the long slow process could not be followed unless his vision were shared by the reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the central subject is a character's internal revolution, choose a focalization that lets the reader share that character's evolving perception; the reader must see the material through the character's eyes for the moral/emotional change to register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer interior/psychological presentation over external dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: “Strether's real situation... his grand adventure is not expressed in its incidents. These, as they are devised by the author, are secondary, they are the extension of the moral event that takes place in the breast of the ambassador, his change of mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the story's core is a moral or mental event, treat incidents as secondary—structure the work to foreground consciousness and impression rather than plot-action alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not render inner life by external report or omniscient exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Only the brain behind his eyes can be aware of the colour of his experience... Nothing that any one else could discern... would give the full sense of the eventful life he is leading within.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid explaining a character's internal states by outside narration or omniscient summary; rely on the character's subjective impressions and the enactment of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize thought via surface images and momentary ripples
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must see for ourselves, the author must so arrange matters that Strether's thought will all be made intelligible by a direct view of its surface. The immediate flaw or ripple of the moment, and the next and the next, will then take up the tale...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the workings of mind through fleeting images, sensations, small moments and their sequence rather than by abstract explanation—use contiguous surface manifestations to make inner processes perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid retrospective first-person expository narration for inward change
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the book were cast autobiographically and Strether spoke in person; he could not hold back, he could not heighten the story of his thought with that touch of suspense... In a tale of murder... the murderer... cannot possibly be the narrator...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A knowing first-person narrator tends to reveal all and remove suspense; prefer methods that allow gradual revelation rather than full retrospective accounting by the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from authorial intrusion or giving readers the author's private knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Henry James knows all there is to know of Strether, but he most carefully refrains from using his knowledge. He wishes us to accept nothing from him, on authority — only to watch and learn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feed the reader facts on the authority of the author; withhold the author's privileged knowledge to preserve discovery and dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes/dialogue to supply necessary background instead of lump narration
rubrics_metrics.description: “He himself... calls attention to the way in which a conversation between Strether and Maria Gostrey... puts the reader in possession of all the past facts of the situation which it is necessary for him to know; a scene thus takes the place of that ‘harking back to make up’... which is apt to appear as a lump of narrative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When backstory or facts are necessary, stage them in scenes or dialogue so they emerge organically rather than as summary dumps; let characters' interactions reveal necessary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scenic episodes as dramatic even within a single-character point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: “In these scenic dialogues... the only eyes in the matter are still his, there is no sight of the man himself as his companion sees him... Yet by an easy sleight of hand the author gives him almost the value of an independent person... simply it consists in treating the scene as dramatically as possible — keeping it framed in Strether's vision, certainly, but keeping his consciousness out of sight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can have a single focalizer yet allow scenes to play with an appearance of objectivity by keeping that focalizer’s ongoing interior commentary out of the scene—this allows dialogue and action to have independent dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the dramatic rule to descriptive/pictorial material, not just dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: “The less dramatic, strictly speaking, the subject may be... the more it is needful to heighten its flat, pictorial, descriptive surface by the arts of drama... The dramatic rule is applied more fundamentally; it animates the actual elements of the picture, the description, and makes a drama of these.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When subject matter is pictorial or static, animate descriptions so they function like drama—let descriptions enact tension and change rather than remain flat depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surround facts; imply rather than state directly to preserve discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not to walk straight up to the fact and put it into phrases, but to surround the fact, and so to detach it inviolate — such is Henry James's manner of dramatizing it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circle the important facts with suggestive detail and peripheral glimpses so they emerge in the reader’s mind without blunt announcement; this preserves subtlety and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build solidity of inner life by showing it from multiple surface angles
rubrics_metrics.description: “Solidity, weight, a third dimension, is given to the impression of Milly's unhappy case... By such a method the image will be so raised out of its setting that the stream of vision will wash it on either side... we shape and solidify the flat impression of a sphere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present recurring surface manifestations of inner states in different contexts and in others’ perceptions to give the interior reality depth and three-dimensional presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let scenes embody appeals and moral weight through setting and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of Susan Stringham's visit: the scene’s room, weather, gestures and broken phrases ‘have all contributed; the broken phrases, without touching it, have travelled about it and revealed its contour.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct scenes so that physical surroundings, tone, gestures and partial speech make the ethical or emotional issue present and palpable before any explicit statement is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use restraint: withhold full exposition so the silent drama can play
rubrics_metrics.description: “The author elects to leave Milly, to join company with her friend in the background, and in that most crucial session to reveal nothing of Milly but the glimpse that her friend catches of her in passing... The glimpse, so rendered, tells nothing. But... there is more in her mind than now appears.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint at key moments; reveal only what can be seen or implied in the scene to allow the reader to infer deeper truths rather than being told them outright.
